title: Modes of Convergence Egorov and Lusin

items.title: Convergence almost everywhere relative to a measure
Convergence in measure
Cauchy sequences in measure
Almost uniform convergence
Convergence in L^1(mu)
Convergence in measure determines the limit almost everywhere
items.strategy: If f_n converges in measure to both f and g, then the set {|f-g| > epsilon} sits inside the union of the two bad sets {|f_n-f| > epsilon/2} and {|f_n-g| > epsilon/2}. Let n tend to infinity and then let epsilon descend through 1/m.

items.title: Convergence in L^1(mu) implies convergence in measure
items.strategy: Apply the Chebyshev-Markov inequality to |f_n - f| at threshold epsilon. The measure of the bad set is bounded by epsilon^{-1} times the L^1 error.

items.title: FALSE: convergence in L^1(mu) forces almost-everywhere convergence
items.strategy: Use the typewriter sequence on [0,1]: its L^1 norm tends to zero because the interval lengths go to zero, but each point is hit infinitely often and missed infinitely often.

items.title: Almost uniform convergence implies almost-everywhere convergence and convergence in measure
items.strategy: Intersect the complements of epsilon 2^{-m}-exceptional sets to get a full-measure set of pointwise convergence, and for a fixed threshold split each bad set into a small exceptional set plus the uniform tail.

items.title: On a finite measure space, almost-everywhere convergence implies convergence in measure
items.strategy: For a fixed epsilon, the tail bad sets {|f_n - f| > epsilon} decrease to a null set. Continuity from above turns the finite total measure hypothesis into vanishing measures of those bad sets.

items.title: FALSE: almost-everywhere convergence implies convergence in measure on every measure space
items.strategy: Use the translates of the unit interval on the real line: they converge pointwise almost everywhere to zero, but the bad set at threshold 1/2 always has measure 1.

items.title: On a finite measure space, the truncated L^1 metric metrises convergence in measure
items.strategy: For d(f,g) = integral min{|f-g|,1} dmu, the lower bound epsilon mu(|f-g| > epsilon) <= d gives one direction, while splitting the integral over {|f-g| <= epsilon} and its complement gives the reverse implication on finite total measure.

items.title: Riesz's subsequence theorem for convergence in measure
items.strategy: Choose the least n_k so that mu(|f_n - f| > 2^{-k}) < 2^{-k} for all n >= n_k. The tail unions have summable measures, their limsup is null by continuity from above, and outside it the chosen subsequence is eventually 2^{-k}-close to f.

items.title: Convergence in L^1(mu) has an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Compose L^1 convergence implies convergence in measure with Riesz's subsequence theorem.

items.title: FALSE: convergence in measure implies almost-everywhere convergence
items.strategy: Use the typewriter sequence: the interval lengths shrink so the bad-set measures vanish, but no pointwise limit exists at any point of [0,1].

items.title: Cauchy sequences in measure converge in measure
items.strategy: Choose a rapidly Cauchy subsequence, apply the same tail-union argument as in Riesz to get an almost-everywhere limit, and use the Cauchy condition to pull the whole sequence to that limit in measure.

items.title: Egorov's theorem
items.strategy: For each accuracy level 1/m, the tail bad sets E_{k,m} = union_{j >= k} {|f_j - f| > 1/m} decrease to a null set. Continuity from above is the exact place where finite total measure is used, and the least index k(m) with mu(E_{k(m),m}) < epsilon 2^{-m} produces almost uniform convergence without choice.

items.title: FALSE: Egorov's theorem holds on every measure space
items.strategy: The translates chi_[n,n+1] converge pointwise to zero on the real line, but any set whose complement has finite measure still meets infinitely many full translates, so the convergence is never uniform there.

items.title: On a finite measure space, convergence in measure has an almost-uniformly convergent subsequence
items.strategy: Apply Riesz's subsequence theorem to get almost-everywhere convergence and then apply Egorov on the finite measure space.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, simple functions are continuous on a large closed core
items.strategy: Write the simple function in canonical form. Approximate each measurable level set from inside by a closed set with tiny deficit, and on the resulting closed union each level set is clopen in the subspace, so the restriction is continuous.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, simple approximants to a measurable function can be made uniformly convergent on a large closed set
items.strategy: Take dominated simple approximants to f, use Egorov to get uniform convergence off a small measurable set, then take a closed subset of that good set with almost the same measure and intersect with the closed cores on which each simple approximant is continuous.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, Lusin's theorem on finite-measure subsets of R^n
items.strategy: First reduce to bounded measurable functions by truncating on a large-measure set where |f| is bounded. Then apply the uniform simple-approximation lemma and pass continuity of the restriction through the uniform limit on the closed core.

items.title: Assuming countable choice and dependent choice, a measurable function on a finite-measure subset of R^n agrees there, off a small set, with a continuous function on R^n
items.strategy: Take the closed core from Lusin and extend the restriction by Tietze.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, on a bounded measurable set, Lusin's closed core can be chosen compact
items.strategy: The closed core from Lusin sits inside a bounded subset of R^n, hence Heine-Borel makes it compact.

items.title: FALSE: assuming countable choice, Lusin's theorem says measurable functions are continuous off a null set
items.strategy: The Dirichlet indicator of the irrationals is nowhere continuous, but on a large closed set avoiding a small open cover of the rationals its restriction is constant.

items.title: A uniformly integrable family
On a finite measure space, uniform integrability is equivalent to L^1-boundedness plus uniform absolute continuity
items.strategy: Tail control gives a uniform L^1 bound by splitting at one large cutoff, and then small sets are controlled by the bounded part plus the common tail. Conversely, combine the uniform absolute continuity with one large cutoff and the L^1 bound to control the large-value tails.

items.title: Dominated families are uniformly integrable
items.strategy: Use the integrable majorant g. Its tails control the large-value sets {|f| > M}, and absolute continuity of the integral for g gives the small-set bound used later.

items.title: FALSE: uniform integrability implies domination by one integrable function
items.strategy: Use a uniformly integrable family of disjoint spikes whose tail integrals tend to zero but whose pointwise supremum has divergent integral, so no single integrable majorant can dominate them all.

items.title: A tight family of integrable functions
Vitali convergence theorem on finite and sigma-finite measure spaces
items.strategy: For finite measure, combine convergence in measure with uniform integrability by splitting into a small-value part and a small-measure bad set, using a subsequence only to identify the limit. For the sigma-finite form, tightness first traps almost all mass inside one finite-measure set, where the finite version applies.

items.title: Dominated convergence is a corollary of Vitali's theorem
items.strategy: A dominating integrable function makes the sequence uniformly integrable, and on sigma-finite spaces its own tails also supply tightness. Finite-measure convergence in measure on the trapped core plus small tails then feed the general Vitali theorem.

items.title: Implication table for the main modes of convergence on a finite measure space
items.strategy: Record exactly which implications among almost-everywhere, almost uniform, in measure, and L^1 convergence are proved on this page, and point each failed arrow to the specific witness item that refutes it.

title: Modes of Convergence Egorov and Lusin — Examples

items.title: The typewriter sequence converges in measure and in L^1 but nowhere pointwise
items.strategy: Write the n-th term as the indicator of one dyadic interval in generation k, where the interval length is 2^{-k}. The bad-set measures and the L^1 norms are therefore 2^{-k}, while every point of [0,1] is visited infinitely often and omitted infinitely often.

items.title: The leftmost dyadic intervals give an explicit almost-everywhere Riesz subsequence
items.strategy: Take the first interval in each dyadic generation. Its supports shrink to {0}, so the subsequence converges to zero at every x > 0 and therefore almost everywhere; on [delta,1] it is eventually identically zero, so the convergence is even almost uniform.

items.title: The translates of the unit interval converge almost everywhere to zero but not in measure
items.strategy: For each fixed x, only finitely many translates [n,n+1] contain x, so the values eventually vanish. But for every n the bad set {|f_n| > 1/2} is exactly [n,n+1], which has measure 1.

items.title: The translated unit intervals show that Egorov needs finite total measure
items.strategy: Let f_n = chi_[n,n+1] on the real line. If a measurable set F has finite-measure complement, then infinitely many whole intervals [n,n+1] still meet F, so sup_{x in F} |f_n(x)| stays 1 infinitely often and the convergence is never uniform on F.

items.title: The spikes k chi_(0,1/k) converge almost everywhere and in measure to zero but not in L^1
items.strategy: Away from 0 the supports are eventually empty, and the bad set at threshold epsilon is (0,1/k) once k > epsilon. But every L^1 norm is 1, and the same tail computation shows the family is not uniformly integrable.

items.title: Egorov for x^k on the unit interval
items.strategy: Fix epsilon > 0 and remove the interval (1 - epsilon, 1]. On the closed core [0,1-epsilon] one has x^k <= (1-epsilon)^k for every x, so the convergence to zero is uniform there and the exceptional set has the prescribed measure.

items.title: The Dirichlet function satisfies Lusin's conclusion without being continuous anywhere
items.strategy: Enumerate the rationals in [0,1] and cover the j-th rational by an open interval of length less than epsilon 2^{-j-1}. Their union U has measure less than epsilon, its complement F is closed, and the indicator of the rationals restricts to the constant zero function on F.

items.title: A uniformly integrable family need not admit a single integrable majorant
items.strategy: Choose pairwise disjoint intervals I_k inside [0,1] with length 1/k^2 and set f_k = k chi_{I_k}. The tail integrals are at most 1/k above level k, so the family is uniformly integrable, but any pointwise majorant dominates the disjoint sum sum_k k chi_{I_k}, whose integral is the harmonic series.
